item.title: Ditoka defends Fiji’s diplomatic missions, says performance is measured
item.description: Ditoka defends Fiji’s diplomatic missions, says performance is measured. Minister for Foreign Affairs and External Trade Sakiasi Ditoka has defended Fiji’s overseas diplomatic missions, rejecting suggestions that the country’s diplomats are primarily engaged in receptions and public appearances.
item.content:encoded:
Ditoka defends Fiji’s diplomatic missions, says performance is measured.

Minister for Foreign Affairs and External Trade Sakiasi Ditoka has defended Fiji’s overseas diplomatic missions, rejecting suggestions that the country’s diplomats are primarily engaged in receptions and public appearances.

In a social media statement, Mr Ditoka said Fiji’s diplomatic representation must deliver value for taxpayers, while acknowledging the need for fiscal responsibility.

He said the Government had systems in place to measure the performance of Fiji’s Ambassadors, High Commissioners and diplomatic missions.

“KPIs are very much part of that conversation,” Mr Ditoka said.

“Our missions have internal targets they are required to meet within the Ministry, as well as performance targets that are reported through to the Ministry of National Planning.”

He said the performance of Fiji’s missions would be assessed against those targets, with the Government prepared to strengthen performance where necessary and adjust the country’s diplomatic footprint where required.

Mr Ditoka said diplomacy should not be judged simply by the number of photographs, receptions or public statements generated by Fiji’s representatives overseas.

He said Fiji’s missions played an important role in opening doors for trade and investment, development partnerships, political and security ties, climate and oceans priorities, education, labour mobility and consular support .

“Some results are visible immediately, others only after months or years of quiet engagement,” he said.

Mr Ditoka also defended the attendance of President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu at the United Nations General Assembly, saying the President, as Fiji’s Head of State, had an important role in representing the country internationally.

He said the President would deliver Fiji’s national statement at the UN General Assembly, while Mr Ditoka would attend as Foreign Affairs Minister to handle bilateral meetings and negotiations.

He said Fiji’s Permanent Representative, diplomats and other officials would also support the delegation.

The President is also expected to visit Fiji’s Permanent Mission in New York and the country’s Embassy in Washington to meet staff.

Mr Ditoka said the Government was also focused on strengthening Fiji’s professional foreign service through a new Diplomatic Academy within the Public Service Commission’s FLIPS framework.

He said the academy was being developed alongside established diplomatic academies overseas to provide Fiji’s young diplomats with exposure to other foreign services.

“There’s more work to do — I make no pretence otherwise,” he said.

“But I won’t accept the caricature that our diplomats are simply overseas attending receptions at taxpayers’ expense.”

Mr Ditoka said Fiji was not a wealthy country and its overseas representation needed to remain within its means.

“Taxpayers deserve value for it,” he said, while stressing that fiscal responsibility should not come at the expense of the dignity of Fiji’s national offices.

“There’s a balance between economy and dignity,” he said.

item.title: Turtle and bird guide Paddle for Hope team through challenging journey
item.description: Mr Bhagwan and fellow paddler, Graham Taylor are paddling along the Coral Coast waters. The team has spent its first week paddling from the National Sailing Centre in Suva, stopping at communities including Muaivuso, Togoru, Lomary and Navutulevu , before continuing towards Tagaqe
item.content:encoded:
Mr Bhagwan and fellow paddler, Graham Taylor are paddling along the Coral Coast waters.

The team has spent its first week paddling from the National Sailing Centre in Suva, stopping at communities including Muaivuso, Togoru, Lomary and Navutulevu , before continuing towards Tagaqe

Rev Bhagwan said the five-day journey had been physically demanding, particularly when the team encountered strong winds and currents on Wednesday.

But he said moments of exhaustion were met with what felt like signs of encouragement from nature.

“As we were paddling, getting tired and about to give up, a turtle, a vonu, would pop up as if to encourage us or guide us in the right direction,” he said.

“Or one of the great birds would fly down over us and encourage us, and so it’s been a very special time.”

Rev Bhagwan said the experience had reinforced the spiritual message behind Paddle for Hope — caring for God’s creation and protecting Fiji’s oceans, rivers and coastlines.

He said the team had been warmly received by communities and churches along the way, with members of the Catholic, Methodist and Anglican churches participating in the initiative.

“It’s been a really good five days of paddling, and we are so grateful for all the communities that have supported us along the way,” he said.

Rev Bhagwan said plastic pollution remained a major focus, with the initiative creating opportunities for communities to discuss waste, single-use plastics, recycling and practical ways to protect their environment.

He said the ecumenical nature of the initiative was also significant, bringing different Christian denominations together around a shared responsibility to care for creation.

The Paddle for Hope programme has included coastal clean-ups, recycling training, community talanoa, prayer and reflections on the Season of Creation.

Rev Bhagwan also acknowledged the support of the Pacific Conference of Churches team, land crew and logistics team, who prepare communities and coordinate activities ahead of the paddlers’ arrival.

He paid special tribute to lead paddler Graham Taylor, describing him as the team’s “paddling captain” on the sea.

Rev Bhagwan said the team would continue its journey around Viti Levu with the message “SUP against SUP — Stand Up Paddling Against Single-Use Plastics.”

“The paddle continues,” the team said in its Week One recap, urging communities to protect their waters, reduce waste and inspire action for future generations.

item.title: Pacific leaders endorse regional Labour Ministers Meeting
item.description: The decision was made at the Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau, where leaders also endorsed the associated Business Case and Ministerial Charter, while taking into account the ongoing review through the Regional Review of Architecture. Leaders said labour and workforce governance had emerged as strategic regional priorities, with growing implications for economic resilience, labour mobility, skills d
item.content:encoded:
The decision was made at the Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau, where leaders also endorsed the associated Business Case and Ministerial Charter, while taking into account the ongoing review through the Regional Review of Architecture.

Leaders said labour and workforce governance had emerged as strategic regional priorities, with growing implications for economic resilience, labour mobility, skills development, workforce sustainability and inclusive growth.

They said the new Labour Ministers Meeting would complement existing regional ministerial mechanisms, including the Forum Economic Ministers Meeting (FEMM) and the Forum Trade Ministers Meeting (FTMM).

FEMM provides oversight of regional economic policy and integration, while FTMM oversees regional trade and labour mobility policy.

The Labour Ministers Meeting will provide dedicated regional leadership on labour and workforce priorities.

Leaders said the three mechanisms would strengthen policy coherence, regional coordination and implementation of the Resources and Economic Development priorities under the Pacific Islands Forum’s 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent.

item.title: Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission begins diaspora hearings in NZ
item.description: The hearings, held at the Fiji High Commission’s boardroom on Saturday, September 5, are part of the Commission’s broader efforts to provide Fijians affected by the country’s political upheavals with an opportunity to participate in the national truth and reconciliation process. Commission Chairperson Joaquim “Russuo” da Fonseca said the New Zealand engagement was particularly important because ma
item.content:encoded:
The hearings, held at the Fiji High Commission’s boardroom on Saturday, September 5, are part of the Commission’s broader efforts to provide Fijians affected by the country’s political upheavals with an opportunity to participate in the national truth and reconciliation process.

Commission Chairperson Joaquim “Russuo” da Fonseca said the New Zealand engagement was particularly important because many Fijians who experienced or were affected by political upheavals now live overseas.

“The diaspora engagement therefore provides an avenue for the survivors to engage with the Commission without having to return to Fiji to participate in the truth-telling process,” he said.

The Commission said survivors and witnesses who come forward can recount their experiences directly to the Commission in a confidential, safe and respectful environment.

Participation is voluntary, with the process designed to be survivor-centred.

Mr da Fonseca is conducting the hearings alongside Commissioners Rachna Nath and Rajendra Dass .

The New Zealand visit is being undertaken under the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act 2024 , including Part 2, Section 6, which outlines the Commission’s functions.

These include facilitating safe and conducive spaces for survivors to share their stories, experiences and trauma.

The Commission said the diaspora hearings form an important part of ensuring the voices of Fijians affected by the country’s political upheavals are included in the national truth and reconciliation process.

item.title: Kiran calls for continued mental health support for RFMF servicewomen
item.description: Speaking at the closing of a five-day RFMF Servicewomen Mental Health and Wellbeing Workshop, Minister Kiran said servicewomen worked in demanding environments while also carrying responsibilities within their families and communities. “Supporting your wellbeing means recognising and valuing the whole person behind the uniform,” she said.
item.content:encoded:
Speaking at the closing of a five-day RFMF Servicewomen Mental Health and Wellbeing Workshop, Minister Kiran said servicewomen worked in demanding environments while also carrying responsibilities within their families and communities.

“Supporting your wellbeing means recognising and valuing the whole person behind the uniform,” she said.

The workshop, held under the theme “Breaking the Cycles,” provided servicewomen with an opportunity to discuss trauma, mental health and healing, while building confidence to recognise distress and seek support for themselves and their colleagues.

Minister Kiran acknowledged the contribution of Fiji’s servicewomen to United Nations peacekeeping missions, humanitarian operations and disaster response.

She said their professionalism, courage and ability to build trust with vulnerable communities had earned Fiji international respect.

However, she said military service could come with a significant personal cost.

Exposure to conflict, danger and the suffering of others could leave deep and unseen wounds, she said, which could also affect families and relationships when personnel returned home.

“We cannot expect you to protect others if we fail to provide the psychological armour you need to protect yourselves and your loved ones,” Minister Kiran said.

She said mental health and wellbeing were essential to operational readiness, discipline, leadership and sustained performance.

The Minister also highlighted pressures that servicewomen could face, including family responsibilities, harassment, workplace discrimination, domestic violence and climate-related emergencies.

She said continued support was needed to strengthen resilience, leadership, peer support and early identification of risks.

Minister Kiran encouraged the servicewomen to continue their healing journey and help ensure every woman and peacekeeper had access to appropriate support.

She congratulated the participants on completing the workshop and thanked them for their service to Fiji.

item.title: Airline sets booking record
item.description: FIJI Airways recorded more than 14,000 bookings on September 2, its highest single-day total in the airline’s 75-year history. The figure surpassed the previous record set in 2023 and was recorded during the airline’s global 75th Anniversary Sale.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI Airways recorded more than 14,000 bookings on September 2, its highest single-day total in the airline’s 75-year history.

The figure surpassed the previous record set in 2023 and was recorded during the airline’s global 75th Anniversary Sale.

Fiji Airways managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the result reflected continued demand for travel to Fiji.

“This is our best booking day ever,” Mr Scurrah said.

The booking record comes as Fiji’s tourism sector continues to grow.

Fiji Bureau of Statistics data shows 105,791 visitors arrived in Fiji in July, the first month in which arrivals exceeded 100,000.

Visitor arrivals for the year to July were 4.3 per cent higher than during the same period in 2025.

Business-class bookings were 17 per cent higher on September 2 than on the same day last year, while group bookings nearly doubled.

Fiji Airways has also expanded its network, recently adding the Gold Coast to its Australian schedule. New services to Nouméa, New Caledonia, are scheduled to begin later this month.

The national airline carries a significant share of visitors travelling to Fiji and is a major employer in the country.

Mr Scurrah said the increase in bookings would support activity across the tourism sector.

item.title: Workshop reviews waste sector target
item.description: FIJI’s waste sector accounts for about 9.7 per cent of the country’s total greenhouse gas emissions, prompting the Government to strengthen systems for measuring and monitoring emissions. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change held a Waste Sector Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) Targets, Mitigation Measures and Monitoring Workshop at the University of the South Pacific’s Statham Ca
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’s waste sector accounts for about 9.7 per cent of the country’s total greenhouse gas emissions, prompting the Government to strengthen systems for measuring and monitoring emissions.

The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change held a Waste Sector Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) Targets, Mitigation Measures and Monitoring Workshop at the University of the South Pacific’s Statham Campus on Thursday.

The workshop brought together representatives from government ministries, development partners, municipal councils and other stakeholders to review waste sector targets under Fiji’s NDC 3.0.

Methane from landfills, wastewater treatment facilities, industries and farms are among the sources contributing to emissions from the sector.

Director of Climate Change Senivasa Waqairamasi said stronger action in the waste sector could provide direct benefits to communities.

A key focus was strengthening Fiji’s Monitoring, Reporting and Verification framework to improve the measurement of emissions reductions and track the effectiveness of mitigation measures.

Participants reviewed proposed monitoring protocols and indicators, including institutional responsibilities and procedures for collecting and sharing data.

The initiative is supported by the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, the Center for Clean Air Policy and ImplementaSur.

The improved monitoring system will support implementation of Fiji’s NDC 3.0 waste-sector targets and help guide future climate investment and policy decisions.

item.title: Process exposes 13 ghost officers
item.description: EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro has confirmed that 13 officers were identified as ghost employees following a payroll verification exercise by the Ministry of Education. The exercise was conducted in response to recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report concerning former ministry employees who continued to receive salaries during the 2024 financial year.
item.content:encoded:
EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro has confirmed that 13 officers were identified as ghost employees following a payroll verification exercise by the Ministry of Education.

The exercise was conducted in response to recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report concerning former ministry employees who continued to receive salaries during the 2024 financial year.

Mr Radrodro said payroll verification was an established process to ensure employment records were accurate and public funds were paid only to legitimate employees.

The exercise also resulted in the cessation of salaries for 134 officers in Pay 18/2026 after the ministry identified outstanding permanent appointment documentation.

The affected teachers had been issued permanent appointment contracts through the Fiji Education Management Information System (FEMIS) in 2025 but had not returned signed contracts for processing and updating of employment records.

Mr Radrodro said the teachers continued to receive salaries until Pay 18/2026 despite the required documentation remaining outstanding.

The verification also identified other employment discrepancies. In one case, a former teacher whose contract expired on January 26, 2025, continued receiving salary payments until Pay 18/2026 after leaving the ministry.

The exercise further found that some affected teachers had not renewed their Fiji Teachers Registration Authority (FTRA) licences as required under the FTRA Act.

Mr Radrodro urged officers to complete and return mandatory employment documents and maintain valid FTRA licences.

He also advised employees to raise employment matters through established ministry channels rather than social media.

Mr Radrodro reminded officers of their obligations under the Civil Service Code of Conduct.
